We also attempted to replicate the well-established associative-priming effect using a
visual lexical decision task (e.g., de Groot, 1984, 1987; Neely, 1967, 1977). This task was
included to confirm the reliability of our experimental procedure, such as the statistical
methodology and the seriousness of the participants. The task and the stimuli were provided by

(2015) as a methodological and participant-motivation reliability check. No specific empirical finding from De Groot (1984) (which examined combined effects of the proportion of related prime-target pairs and stimulus-onset asynchrony) is retested. No prior adjudication/state files exist.

corrected_value.title: Rule breaking in adolescence and entrepreneurial status: An empirical investigation.

decisions.quote: Drawing from Zhang and Arvey's retrospective study [Zhang, Z. & Arvey, R.D. (2009). Rule breaking in adolescence and entrepreneurial status: An empirical investigation. Journal of Business Venturing, 24(5), 436–447], which found a link between entrepreneurship status of male adults and their recalled early antisocial rule-breaking behavior in adolescence, the present study utilized prospective longitudinal data from a Swedish cohort study to clarify the connection between antisocial rule-breaking, crime, and entrepreneurship by applying a developmental perspective. Regression results, which controlled for early socioeconomic background and intellectual competencies, indeed identified early antisocial rule-breaking behavior in adolescence as a valid positive predictor of a subsequent entrepreneurial career in adulthood in men (but not in women).
decisions.reason: The title and abstract explicitly establish that this study is a replication and extension retesting the empirical finding of Zhang & Arvey (2009), 'Rule breaking in adolescence and entrepreneurial status: An empirical investigation', Journal of Business Venturing, 24(5), 436-447—specifically, the positive association between adolescent antisocial rule-breaking behavior and adult entrepreneurial status in men—using 37-year prospective longitudinal Swedish cohort data and confirming the positive prediction in men via regression analyses. The sole shipped original (input_row_index 1322, 10.1016/j.obhdp.2009.07.002) is Zhang, Zyphur, Narayanan, Arvey, Chaturvedi, Avolio, Lichtenstein, & Larsson (2009), 'The genetic basis of entrepreneurship: Effects of gender and personality' in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 110(2), 93-107, which is a distinct behavioral-genetics twin study of heritability, gender, and personality rather than an alternate report of the 2-author rule-breaking study. No prior adjudication/state files exist.

corrected_value.authors: Santiago, J. L., Hanley, G. P., Moore, K., & Jin, C. S.
corrected_value.title: The generality of interview-informed functional analyses: Systematic replications in school and home.

decisions.quote:
We replicated and extended Hanley
et al. (2014) and Santiago et al. (2016). We
demonstrated the positive effects of stregthening FCRs, tolerance responses, and engagement
with reinforcers identiﬁed via interview and
analysis on problem behaviors with two young
children diagnosed with ASD.
decisions.reason: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion that they replicated and extended both Hanley et al. (2014) and Santiago et al. (2016), empirically retesting Santiago et al.'s (2016) home-based, non-BCBA-implemented interview-informed synthesized contingency analysis and skill-based treatment with two children with ASD in their homes and demonstrating large reductions in problem behavior, increases in functional communication and delay-tolerance responses, and high caregiver social validity. The only shipped row (input_row_index 2309, 10.1002/jaba.106) represents Hanley, Jin, Vanselow, & Hanratty (2014) in Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis, 47(1), 16-36 (the initial clinic-based study), whereas Santiago, Hanley, Moore, & Jin (2016) in Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, 46(3), 797-811 (10.1007/s10803-015-2617-0) is a separate published study with different participants, home/school settings, and implementers, not an alternate report of Hanley et al. (2014). No prior adjudication/state files exist.
